title: Are boutique R&D tax credit companies legitimate or a scam?
description: Boutique R&D tax credit firms are generally legitimate advisers on the real federal credit, but the IRS does not certify them, so each must be vetted.
summary: Boutique R&D tax credit firms in the United States are generally legitimate advisers working on the real federal research credit under I.R.C. §41, not a scam by category. However, the IRS does not certify these firms, and taxpayers bear the penalty risk, so each firm must be vetted on its process, written fee terms and audit-defense support.

body.text: Boutique R&D tax credit firms in the United States are generally legitimate advisers working on the real federal research credit under I.R.C. §41, not a scam by category. However, the IRS does not certify these firms, and taxpayers bear the penalty risk, so each firm must be vetted on its process, written fee terms and audit-defense support.
Prepared November 10, 2026, with United States law as the primary jurisdiction.
1. Short answer

Analysis: Specialist ("boutique") R&D tax credit firms are not a scam by category. The incentives they work on are real, government-backed programs, and most claimants use an adviser of some kind. However, neither the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) nor the UK tax authority (HMRC) certifies these firms as a group, and no federal license exists for "R&D tax credit specialists" as such. Official data shows that a large share of claims, including claims prepared with specialist help, have been non-compliant. Whether a particular firm is legitimate depends on how it works: how it gathers evidence, how it charges, and what support it gives if the claim is examined.

In the United States, the stakes of choosing badly fall mainly on the taxpayer. The taxpayer signs the return or refund claim, bears any disallowance with interest, and can face accuracy-related penalties under I.R.C. §6662 or, for an excessive refund or credit claim made without reasonable cause, the 20% erroneous-claim penalty under I.R.C. §6676. The preparer can face its own penalties under I.R.C. §6694, but those do not relieve the taxpayer of the underpayment. A firm's legitimacy therefore has to be judged by whether its work will hold up under IRS examination, not by whether it can produce a large credit figure.
2. The incentives are real, and so is the scrutiny
2.1 The underlying programs

In the United States the research credit is the credit for increasing research activities under I.R.C. §41, claimed on IRS Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities. The credit rests on the four-part test in §41(d): the expenses must be eligible for treatment as research and experimental expenditures, the research must be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature, the information must be intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component, and substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation. Since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21, signed July 4, 2025), §41(d) cross-refers to domestic research or experimental expenditures under new I.R.C. §174A, which restored immediate expensing of domestic research costs for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 (see section 4.3).

Comparable incentives exist elsewhere. According to the OECD, income-based R&D tax incentives cut firms' tax liabilities by 35% on average across OECD countries in 2024, and these incentives are used in most OECD countries and other major economies. A firm that helps a business claim a statutory credit is providing an ordinary professional service; the question is whether it does so accurately.
2.2 UK claim volumes

HMRC's accredited official statistics (September 2025) confirm this. They give a provisional estimate of 46,950 claims for 2023 to 2024, made up of 36,885 SME scheme claims and 10,065 RDEC scheme claims, down 26% on the previous year. Other reporting on the same release puts the SME-scheme fall at 31% and the RDEC fall at 5%.

Update: HMRC's September 2026 publication (updated September 29, 2026) gives provisional figures for 2024 to 2025: 40,325 claims, a further 17% decrease. Total support claimed rose 5%, to £8.2 billion, and 6% of claims accounted for 69% of the total value claimed. HMRC warns that the 2024 to 2025 figures are provisional, that claims for that year can still be submitted after the publication's cut-off date, and that the new merged scheme and ERIS make SME figures not comparable with earlier years.

Relevance to US readers: The IRS does not publish an equivalent error-rate study for §41 claims. US readers should treat the UK data as evidence of how the specialist-adviser market can behave, not as a measure of US compliance rates.
2.3 Error versus fraud

HMRC's own report (Approach to Research and Development tax reliefs 2023 to 2024, published October 30, 2024) does not give a formal error-versus-fraud split. What it says about its second Mandatory Random Enquiry Programme (MREP2) is narrower: fraud indicators appeared in fewer than 10% of cases examined, and those cases made up around 5% of the total value claimed. HMRC concludes that most non-compliance is due to other behaviors. Corrected framing: about 90% of examined cases showed no fraud indicators. HMRC does not state that 90% of non-compliance is "misinterpretation."

Analysis: For the "legitimate or scam" question this distinction matters. If most non-compliance comes from poor understanding of the rules rather than deliberate fraud, the main risk with an adviser is incompetence or over-aggressive interpretation, not outright deception. That is a risk a taxpayer can test for through the due-diligence steps in section 7.
2.4 First-time claimants
HMRC's report confirms that 64% of the value of first-time claims was non-compliant. It also says 46% of claims from that group were wholly non-compliant (MREP2, 2021 to 2022 claims).

The US parallel is that first-time and amended-return claims receive particular attention from the IRS. Since January 10, 2022, a refund claim that includes a §41 credit must carry specified supporting information to be treated as a valid claim at all (section 4.2). Many boutique firms market "look-back" studies that claim the credit for open prior years by amended return, which places that work squarely within these requirements.
2.5 What HMRC says about advisers: directly relevant to the "scam" question
HMRC's October 2024 report includes findings that bear directly on whether specialist firms can be trusted.

items: More than 90% of claimants have an authorized agent acting for them.
HMRC says it does not regulate tax agents, including those who advise on R&D claims.
In MREP2, about half of claims used a specialist R&D agent. Non-compliance by value was slightly higher for those claims (28%) than for claims made without one (21%).
HMRC acknowledges that some agents give poor or incorrect advice about what clients can claim.
Since 2023, HMRC's R&D Anti-Abuse Unit has worked with the advertising regulator to remove false advertising by agents who claim to be HMRC-approved.

body.text: US regulatory position: The US position is similar in effect. The IRS regulates practice before it through Treasury Department Circular 230 (31 C.F.R. Part 10), which governs attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents and others who represent taxpayers. However, the D.C. Circuit held in Loving v. IRS, 742 F.3d 1013 (D.C. Cir. 2014), that the IRS lacks statutory authority under 31 U.S.C. §330 to regulate ordinary return preparers, and the district court in Ridgely v. Lew, 55 F. Supp. 3d 89 (D.D.C. 2014), applied the same reasoning to the preparation of ordinary refund claims. As a result, an R&D credit firm whose staff are not attorneys, CPAs or enrolled agents can prepare credit studies and amended-return claims without any IRS credential. The IRS does not "approve" or "certify" R&D credit firms, and any firm that advertises IRS approval is misdescribing its status.

Analysis: The fair conclusion is a mixed one. Specialist agents are not proof of a compliant claim, and in HMRC's sample they did not lower non-compliance on average. Advertised "approval" by a tax authority is itself a warning sign. Some firms are legitimate and some are not, so each firm has to be vetted on its own merits.
3. Warning signs of a high-risk R&D firm

cells: 1. Using industry averages or shortcut methods to calculate the credit

Confirmed in the cited adviser article, which lists using industry averages or other shortcut methods to calculate the credit as a reason to ask more questions or get another opinion. This is professional commentary, not IRS guidance. Primary authority points the same way: Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(3) and (b) apply the four-part test separately to each business component, and §1.41-4(d) requires taxpayers to retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that expenditures claimed are eligible. Estimates detached from actual projects are difficult to reconcile with those requirements.
2. Not interviewing technical staff or reviewing project documentation

Confirmed in the same article, which flags failing to interview staff and obtain documentation from them. It also notes that minimal time spent usually means minimal supporting documentation. For refund claims, the IRS now requires the taxpayer to identify the individuals who performed each research activity and the information each sought to discover (section 4.2), which cannot be done responsibly without technical interviews.
3. Weak technical narrative

The Tax Adviser (October 2025) notes growing pressure in software to separate qualified development from routine maintenance. In the United States, §41(d)(4) excludes, among other things, research after the beginning of commercial production, adaptation of an existing business component, and surveys and routine data collection, and internal-use software must also meet the additional requirements of Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(6). In the UK, HMRC says it continues to see many misunderstandings of what counts as R&D under the DSIT guidelines. The current UK guidelines were issued on March 7, 2023 and are published by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT). HMRC now calls them the DSIT guidelines.
4. No project-level costing

The Tax Adviser says the credit now demands rigorous cost tracking on a per-project basis. It notes that architecture and engineering (A&E) work is often challenged because of dual-function activities, and that manufacturing scrutiny focuses on tooling, prototyping and custom fabrication. See section 4 for what Form 6765 requires.
5. Fee structures that are not transparent

The cited adviser article notes that R&D claim providers often work on a contingency basis to make their offer more attractive. US legal context: Circular 230 §10.27 generally bars practitioners from charging a contingent fee for preparing an original tax return, but after Ridgely v. Lew the IRS cannot enforce that restriction against fees for preparing ordinary refund claims (amended returns filed before an examination begins). Section 10.27 also allows contingent fees for services connected with an IRS examination of, or challenge to, a return or claim. Contingent fees for R&D refund studies are therefore lawful in many settings; what matters is whether the fee basis is disclosed and written into the engagement letter.
6. No support if the claim is examined

The concern is reasonable, but no regulator states it as a rule. Whether defense costs are covered depends on each firm's engagement terms (see section 6.4). Only attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents and certain other individuals listed in Circular 230 §10.3 may represent a taxpayer before the IRS in an examination, so a firm without such staff cannot personally defend the claim it prepared.

items: An "audit risk" chart scoring specialist firms 15, generalist CPAs 65 and DIY claims 85.
A chart saying a compliant claim is 60% technical narrative, 25% financial calculation and 15% compliance review.
The statement that "most boutique firms email spreadsheets unencrypted."
The characterization of boutique firms as "mostly accountants" with an "aggressive" risk approach.

body.text: None of these figures or generalizations comes from any data source, and this report does not rely on them.
4. US documentation standards: Form 6765
4.1 Form 6765 redesign
The IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Revised December 2025, for use with the January 2025 revision of the form) confirm this, with an important qualification on timing and scope.

cells: Section G (business component information)
Optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026. Required for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to the exemptions below. Amended returns follow separate rules.
Who is exempt from Section G

(a) Qualified small businesses under §41(h)(3) that check the box to elect the reduced payroll tax credit; or (b) taxpayers whose controlled-group total QREs on line 48 are $1.5 million or less, whose average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are $50 million or less, and who report the credit on an original return.
Labor classification

Wages are split into those for people performing qualified services, those for direct supervision (immediate, first-line management of qualified research; supervision by higher-level managers does not count), and those for direct support (for example, a laboratory worker cleaning research equipment or a clerk compiling research data; general administrative services and services that only indirectly benefit research do not count). Officers' wages included in the qualified wages are reported separately on line 38, with state law determining who is an officer.
Payroll tax election for qualified small businesses

The election cannot exceed $500,000 per tax year. A qualified small business generally has gross receipts under $5 million for the tax year and no gross receipts for any tax year before the five-tax-year period ending with the current year. The election must be made on a timely filed original return, including extensions, and cannot be made for a year if it was made for five or more preceding tax years.

body.text: In fact Section G becomes mandatory only for tax years beginning after 2025, and many smaller claimants are exempt. For calendar-year taxpayers, the first return that must include Section G is the 2026 return, normally filed in 2027.
Analysis: The IRS instructions set out what has to be reported. They do not say who must prepare it.
4.2 Refund claims: the "five items of information"

In Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F (released October 15, 2021), the IRS Office of Chief Counsel concluded that, to satisfy the specificity requirement of Treas. Reg. §301.6402-2(b)(1), a research credit refund claim must at a minimum identify the business components to which the claim relates; for each business component, the research activities performed, the individuals who performed them, and the information each sought to discover; and the total qualified employee wage, supply and contract research expenses for the claim year. The requirement applies to claims postmarked on or after January 10, 2022. A one-year transition period, which ended January 9, 2023, allowed 45 days to perfect a deficient claim; claims filed after that date do not receive that opportunity.

In June 2024 the IRS modified these requirements and waived the need to provide two of the items (the individuals who performed each activity and the information each sought to discover) at the time of filing, while reserving the right to request them if the claim is examined. The current Form 6765 instructions state that a refund claim on an amended return or administrative adjustment request (AAR) that includes a §41 credit must include the specified information to be considered valid, and that e-filed claims carry it as an attachment named "Form6765ClaimInformation.pdf." Column 49(f) is required for amended-return claims that add or increase the credit.

Analysis: A firm that offers to prepare prior-year refund claims without collecting business-component detail is preparing claims the IRS can treat as invalid without examining their merits. This is a concrete, checkable test of competence.
4.3 Section 174A and the credit

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act created I.R.C. §174A, which allows domestic research or experimental expenditures to be deducted in the year paid or incurred for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, or, at the taxpayer's election, capitalized and amortized over not less than 60 months. Foreign research expenditures remain subject to 15-year amortization under §174. The Act also amended §280C(c) so that the domestic expenditure deduction or capitalized amount is reduced by the amount of the §41 credit. Eligible small businesses (average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less) could elect to apply §174A retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, with the election required within one year of enactment. These rules affect how a credit claim interacts with the taxpayer's deductions, so a competent adviser must coordinate the §41 credit with §174A and §280C(c) rather than computing the credit in isolation.
5. Location rules that a competent adviser must apply

items: United States: Under I.R.C. §41(d)(4)(F), research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico or any US possession is not qualified research. Since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, foreign research expenditures also remain subject to 15-year amortization under §174, while domestic expenditures are deductible under §174A. An adviser who counts offshore development costs toward the US credit is misapplying the statute.

Australia: According to the ATO, generally only R&D activities conducted in Australia qualify. Overseas activities qualify only if the Department of Industry, Science and Resources makes an overseas finding. Among other conditions, spending on the overseas activities must be less than spending on the related activities conducted in Australia (business.gov.au).

UK: For accounting periods beginning on or after April 1, 2024, relief for contracted-out R&D and externally provided workers is generally restricted to activity carried out in the UK, with limited exceptions.

body.text: 6. Testing the "benchmark" firm
6.1 Specialization, age and size

items: Exclusive focus: The firm's website says it provides only R&D tax credit services and states, "We do one thing, and we do it better than anyone else because it's all we do."

Founded 1984: The firm says it was founded in 1984 as Reed & Co. Conflict: the BBB profile for the Fort Worth, Texas business lists a start date of October 14, 2014 (11 years in business). This report could not resolve the difference. The 1984 date may refer to a predecessor entity.
"Largest" specialist firm: The firm's own pages describe it as "one of the largest" specialist R&D tax credit firms in the US.
All 50 states: The firm says it provides federal and state preparation and audit services to all 50 states (self-reported).

body.text: 6.2 Independence

The firm states that it is "not connected to any CPA firm" and that it will never receive third-party funding. Both statements are self-reported. Under US rules, a CPA firm that both audits a client's financial statements and prepares its tax positions is subject to AICPA and, for public companies, SEC and PCAOB independence rules, but nothing in federal tax law makes a CPA-affiliated R&D practice less reliable than an independent one.
6.3 Fees: the firm's own pages conflict

The firm says its fees are "the most transparent in the market." That is a marketing claim and cannot be verified. Its published hourly rates of $195 to $395 for preparation and audit services are confirmed on its website. On success or contingency fees, its pages disagree:

Analysis: A business vetting any firm, this one included, should get the fee basis confirmed in the signed engagement letter rather than relying on website text. Where a contingent fee is proposed for an original return, the taxpayer should also ask whether the preparer is a Circular 230 practitioner, since §10.27 generally prohibits that arrangement for practitioners even though, after Ridgely, it does not reach ordinary refund claims.
6.4 Review process, technology and audit-cost coverage

items: Six-Eye Review: The firm describes a mandatory internal review of every claim by a qualified engineer, a scientist, and a CPA or Enrolled Agent (self-reported; no independent verification of how it works in practice).

TaxTrex: The firm says its AI agents extract contemporaneous evidence "throughout the year" and list automated surveys and secure storage among its features. The firm's AI page does not mention time-stamping. Its "90 minutes" figure refers to processing documentation, and another firm page says self-claiming takes "just 90 minutes." Neither page says "under 90 minutes." No IRS guidance endorses any particular software for substantiating the credit; the standard remains the record-keeping requirement of Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d) and, for refund claims, the information requirements in section 4.2.
"Compliance ready" case study: The Louisiana page's case study (Wino Incorporated) does describe the client as "compliance ready," but it does not mention TaxTrex.

creditARMOR: The firm describes it as an R&D tax credit insurance and AI-driven risk management platform that covers defense expenses, including CPA, tax attorney and specialist consultant fees. The firm's pages do not say who underwrites the insurance or whether it is included in standard fees.
ISO 27001: The firm says it is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (self-reported; no certificate was checked).
Staff: The firm describes its operational teams as tax CPAs, tax attorneys and industry-specific engineers.

body.text: 6.5 Independent record

The BBB profile confirms an A+ rating and BBB accreditation since December 6, 2024. BBB states that customer reviews are not used in calculating its rating, so an A+ shows how the business deals with BBB. It is not an assessment of the quality of its tax work. For US firms, a more relevant independent check is whether the individuals who will sign or defend the claim hold active credentials: CPA licenses can be checked with the issuing state board of accountancy, attorney admissions with the state bar, and enrolled agent status with the IRS.
7. Due-diligence checklist for any boutique R&D firm (analysis)

items: Process: Will the firm interview your technical staff, review project documents and build project-level costs, rather than relying on averages?

Technical and tax review: Who reviews the claim, and what are their qualifications? Ask for this in writing; don't accept marketing descriptions alone. Confirm that the signer holds an active CPA license, bar admission or enrolled agent status.
Fees in writing: Is the fee fixed, hourly or contingent? Is audit or examination support included or billed separately? Get both stated in the engagement letter.
Defense support: If insurance is offered, who underwrites it, what does it exclude, and what does it cost? Who will represent you before the IRS, and are they eligible to do so under Circular 230?

Claims of official approval: Treat any claim to be "HMRC-approved" or IRS-endorsed as a warning sign. HMRC says it does not regulate R&D agents and has acted against false advertising of approval, and the IRS does not certify R&D credit firms.

Current rules: Is the firm working to the current rules: Form 6765 Section G timing and exemptions in the US, the five-items requirement for refund claims, the §174A and §280C(c) changes, the April 2024 overseas restrictions in the UK, and overseas findings in Australia?

body.text: 8. Conclusion

Analysis: Boutique R&D tax credit firms are a legitimate category of professional adviser working on real government incentives. They are not a scam as a class. But the official data rules out treating any specialist firm as safe by default. HMRC does not regulate these agents, has found false claims of HMRC approval, and in its random enquiry sample found slightly higher non-compliance by value among claims prepared with specialist agents. In the United States, the IRS does not certify R&D credit firms, cannot regulate fees for ordinary refund claims after Ridgely v. Lew, and places the burden of substantiation and the risk of penalties under §§6662 and 6676 on the taxpayer. Legitimacy has to be established firm by firm, from verifiable process, written fee terms and clear defense arrangements.
